slides.c: 6 October 1866: the West Pier opens. Designed by Eugenius Birch.
Cast-iron columns screwed into the seabed. 1,115 feet of promenade.
Gas lamps with serpent designs, toll houses, glass screens against the wind.
The pierhead is extended and a pavilion for 1,400 people is added.
Fresh air gives way to entertainment.
Spencer Gore paints it. 1910–11: about 1.5 million visitors.
20 April 1916: the concert hall opens. About 2 million visitors in 1918–19.
1970: the pierhead closes for safety. 1975: the whole pier closes to the public.
1982: Britain's only Grade I listed pier. 1987: the Great Storm. 1991: shore access removed.
2001: English Heritage names it the most at-risk Grade I structure in England.
December 2002: a storm drops the walkway to the pavilion into the sea. January 2003: the concert hall falls.
28 March 2003: the pavilion burns. 11–12 May 2003: a second fire takes most of the concert hall. Both thought to be arson.
June 2004: the middle collapses. English Heritage declares it beyond repair.
February 2010: partly demolished, partly to make way for the i360 tower.
February 2014: storms split the pier in half.
February 2016: another section collapses.
The starlings still come at dusk.
A skeleton in the sea, still standing, mostly.
DANGER. Keep away.
The most recent photograph in this gallery. Ten months before the storm.

now.c: Storm Austen. More of the West Pier collapsed into the sea. Which section, and how much remains, has not been officially stated.
now.c2: “Disappear it will.” West Pier Trust: stay at a safe distance.
